description: We are the Cibinauts, engineers from Sibiu, Romania, named after the Cibin river that runs through our city. With backgrounds in computer engineering and topography and daily work with software and AI, we are drawn to mapping terrain and making sense of data on the Moon and Mars: a child's dream.
summary:
Twinterra finds new places on Earth that can stand in for the Moon and Mars, and explains why each one works and where it falls short.

We combined open NASA and partner-agency data (MODIS, GLDAS and ETOPO for Earth; MOLA, TES, Mars Odyssey, SWIM, CRISM and the Mars Climate Database for Mars; LOLA, Diviner, Kaguya and Lunar Prospector for the Moon) into comparable features: temperature swing and mean, elevation, slope, roughness, albedo, mineral signals, water/ice and landing safety. Research-backed weights balance geology, terrain, temperature, water and operations, and a similarity score (0–100 %) compares places feature by feature, skipping vegetated land and permanent ice.

The interactive two-globe tool works both ways. Start from Earth to find the Martian or lunar twins of our strongest Earth sites, or start from a real candidate site (Mars exploration zones and caves, lunar pits) to find where on Earth to rehearse it. Globes show NASA Trek imagery plus elevation, temperature-swing, water/ice and landing-safety layers. Each pair opens a side-by-side comparison in physical units, including what Earth cannot reproduce, such as air pressure. A similarity heatmap and “Choose your mission” sliders reweight the search for water hunting, thermal testing, rover operations or geology training.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Twinterra is an interactive two-globe web tool. It searches the whole Earth for new places that resemble sites on Mars or the Moon, and for each match it explains what makes it analogous and what does not.

  1. Open data.
    • Earth, through NASA Earthdata: MODIS land-surface temperature (MOD11C3/MYD11C3), surface reflectance (MCD43C4) and vegetation index (MOD13C2), GLDAS soil moisture and ETOPO 2022 elevation.
    • Mars: MOLA topography, TES albedo, Mars Odyssey GRS water, SWIM subsurface ice, CRISM mineral indices and the Mars Climate Database.
    • The Moon: LOLA topography and albedo, Diviner temperatures, Kaguya iron oxide and Lunar Prospector hydrogen.
    • day–night temperature swing and mean temperature;
    • elevation, slope and roughness;
    • albedo and a mineral signal;
    • water/ice;
    • landing safety and trafficability.
    • vegetated land and permanent ice are excluded;
    • Earth sites are kept at least 300 km apart, so results cover different regions;
    • at least 40 % of the weight must have data on both worlds.
    • Start from Earth to find the Martian or lunar twins of our strongest Earth sites.
    • Start from a real candidate site (145 Mars cave candidates, Mars exploration zones, 150 lunar pits) to find where on Earth it could be rehearsed.
    • The globes stream NASA Trek imagery, plus layers for elevation, albedo, temperature swing, water/ice and landing safety.
    • Selecting a site shows its top three matches. A “Side by side” sheet compares every feature on both worlds in physical units. It also lists what Earth cannot reproduce, such as low air pressure or CO₂ frost.
    • A similarity heatmap colours all of Mars or the Moon by how closely each place matches the selected Earth site, and a star marks the best place.
    • “Choose your mission” sliders reweight the search for water hunting, thermal testing, rover operations or geology training.

What benefits does it have?

  • Systematic and repeatable. Every land cell on Earth is scored with the same transparent formula, so the search doesn’t depend on sites that are already famous.
  • Explainable. Each match shows which features agree, which don’t, where data is sparse (“low confidence”), and what no place on Earth can reproduce.
  • Fits the purpose. Analog quality depends on what you want to test, and the mission sliders show how the best site changes.
  • Lightweight. It is a static web app that runs in any browser with no server. The heatmap is computed in the browser in about 10 ms from small precomputed grids of about 1.2 MB per body.
  • Extensible. All weights live in one configuration file, so a new dataset becomes one more feature.

What is the intended impact?
We want to help mission teams, researchers and educators find more diverse, more accessible and better-matched field-test sites for Artemis and future Mars missions. Testing equipment where conditions match the actual target site lowers risk. The tool can also reveal regions, including ones in countries rarely used for analog research, that have never been considered. It also lets the public explore how Earth relates to other worlds.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

  • Python 3.13: NumPy, SciPy, rasterio/GDAL, pyhdf (MODIS HDF4), pyproj, scikit-learn (feature scaling), geopandas, and earthaccess (NASA Earthdata Login and CMR).
  • JavaScript: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Three.js (Mars and Moon globes with our own tile streaming), MapLibre GL (Earth globe) and lucide icons.
  • Data services and formats: NASA Earthdata, NASA Trek WMTS tiles, USGS Astrogeology and the PDS. Files are HDF4, NetCDF, PDS3, GeoTIFF and GeoJSON.
  • Hardware and other tools: ordinary laptops (Windows), Git and GitHub, oxlint, and Claude Code as an AI coding assistant. No special hardware was needed.

How is the project creative?

  • It works in both directions: Earth to Mars/Moon, and Mars/Moon to Earth.
  • The similarity heatmap shows that the best twin of a site is often somewhere nobody has looked.
  • The mission sliders turn “is this a good analog?” into “a good analog for what?”
  • Comparing ranks within each world makes data from different instruments comparable.
  • Matching Earth places to Martian caves and lunar pits, which could shelter future crews, links analog research to base planning.
  • The tool is honest about limits: it shows what Earth cannot reproduce as clearly as what matches.

What factors did the team consider?

  • The challenge’s main goal: find new analogs, not rediscover known ones, and explain both the similarities and the differences.
  • Scientific relevance: weights backed by literature, and temperature swing weighted more heavily than mean temperature.
  • Data comparability: different instruments, units and resolutions on each world, handled with rank comparison, coverage thresholds and low-confidence flags.
  • Misleading matches: Antarctica’s permanent ice would otherwise dominate, vegetation rules out a place, and cells above 75° latitude are distorted.
  • Resolution limits: cells are about 11 km on Earth and coarser for planetary data, so results point to regions that still need checking in the field.
  • Usability: a clean interface, physical units and plain-language labels.
    • Earth data for the dimensions that already have weight but no features yet: dust/wind, caves, magnetic field and gravity.
    • Site access and protected areas.
    • Higher-resolution data for shortlisted sites.
